title: Beautify and Refine Embellecer y Refinar

blocks.en: Unit Six · Stage 4: Finishing Touches
blocks.es_reference: Unidad Seis · Etapa 4: Toques Finales

blocks.en: Beautify and Refine
blocks.es_reference: Embellecer y Refinar

blocks.en: Beauty, simplicity, the title, transitions, introduction, conclusion, and the preaching analysis tool.
blocks.es_reference: Belleza, simplicidad, título, transiciones, introducción, conclusión y la herramienta de análisis de predicación.

blocks.en: 6.1 A Touch of Beauty
blocks.es_reference: 6.1 Un Toque de Belleza

blocks.en: Outlines seem to be stronger, and are remembered more easily, when each point is five or fewer words in length. Another important ingredient of beauty is parallelism. With parallelism you try to extend the exact wording of each division for as long as possible. In most instances parallelism helps the hearers to remember the message, and it produces a nicer outline. This may or may not involve alliteration, the repetition of a sound.
blocks.es_reference: Los bosquejos parecen ser más fuertes, y se recuerdan con más facilidad, cuando cada punto tiene cinco palabras o menos de extensión. Otro ingrediente importante de la belleza es el paralelismo. Con el paralelismo se trata de extender la redacción exacta de cada división tanto como sea posible. En la mayoría de los casos el paralelismo ayuda a los oyentes a recordar el mensaje, y produce un bosquejo más agradable. Esto puede o no implicar la aliteración, la repetición de un sonido.

blocks.en: A message is usually stronger if it is in the active voice instead of the passive voice. Voice is a grammatical term used to tell whether the subject of the sentence is acting or receiving the action expressed by the verb. "John the Baptist proclaimed the arrival of Christ" (active) is stronger than "The arrival of Christ was preached by John the Baptist" (passive). Sometimes you may begin with a rough outline in which two of the points are active and one is passive; it may be possible to change the voice of the passive point without changing the meaning. Sometimes the divisions may be reworded so that a nicer outline is developed while retaining the essential integrity of the text.
blocks.es_reference: Los bosquejos parecen ser más fuertes, y se recuerdan más fácilmente, cuando cada punto tiene cinco palabras o menos de longitud. Otro ingrediente importante de la belleza es el paralelismo. Con el paralelismo usted intenta extender el lenguaje exacto de cada división durante el mayor tiempo posible. En la mayoría de los casos el paralelismo ayuda a los oyentes a recordar el mensaje, y produce un bosquejo más bonito. Esto puede o no involucrar la aliteración, la repetición de un sonido.

blocks.es_reference: Mostrar modelo: Refinando el bosquejo de Lucas 15:21-22

blocks.en: 6.2 The Beauty of Simplicity
blocks.es_reference: 6.2 La Belleza de la Simplicidad

blocks.en: For us to use words like justification, spiritual, faith, repentance, righteous, calling, fellowship, conversion, holiness, ordain, sanctification, glorification, propitiation, or redemption is often to miss the mark. Most people in the pew will not understand what we are talking about. Even simpler words like church, letter, faith, or grace will often not communicate. If we are trying to attract people with little or no church background, we must be understandable. It is important therefore to explain in simple terms what we want to say. Jesus managed to communicate important theological concepts with the use of parables.
blocks.es_reference: Para nosotros usar palabras como justificación, espiritual, fe, arrepentimiento, justo, llamado, comunión, conversión, santidad, ordenar, santificación, glorificación, propiciación o redención a menudo es no dar en el blanco. La mayoría de las personas en las bancas no entenderá de qué estamos hablando. Incluso palabras más simples como iglesia, carta, fe o gracia a menudo no comunicarán. Si estamos tratando de atraer a personas con poco o ningún trasfondo eclesial, debemos ser comprensibles. Es importante, por lo tanto, explicar en términos simples lo que queremos decir. Jesús logró comunicar conceptos teológicos importantes con el uso de parábolas.

blocks.en: 6.3 The Finishing Touches — Title, Transition, Introduction
blocks.es_reference: 6.3 Los Toques Finales — Título, Transición, Introducción

blocks.en: A sermon is composed of three primary parts: the introduction, the body, and the conclusion. We have been working primarily on the body up to this point. Now we will insert the finishing touches.
blocks.es_reference: Un sermón se compone de tres partes primarias: la introducción, el cuerpo y la conclusión. Hasta este punto hemos trabajado principalmente en el cuerpo. Ahora insertaremos los toques finales.

blocks.en: Title. The title is the name you give to the sermon — what it is called. The primary purpose for having a title is for advertising the sermon. You are trying to catch the listener's attention. Some pastors post the sermon title on the church sign; others place the title in the bulletin. The title may sometimes be the same as the subject, but this is not always true. Many effective titles relate to human needs: "How to Raise Your Kids," "How to Have a Happy Home," "How to Cope with Stress," "How to Manage Your Money."
blocks.es_reference: Título. El título es el nombre que usted le da al sermón: cómo se llama. El propósito primario de tener un título es anunciar el sermón. Usted está tratando de captar la atención del oyente. Algunos pastores ponen el título del sermón en el letrero de la iglesia; otros lo colocan en el boletín. El título a veces puede ser igual al sujeto, pero esto no siempre es así. Muchos títulos eficaces se relacionan con necesidades humanas: «Cómo criar a sus hijos», «Cómo tener un hogar feliz», «Cómo enfrentar el estrés», «Cómo administrar su dinero».

blocks.en: Transition. The transition is a moving from one section of the sermon to another. You need a transition from the introduction into the body, between the divisions, and in moving from the divisions to the conclusion. The major transition is going from the introduction to the body. This transition should include the subject and may be stated, "Let us examine (transition) some answers as to who Christ is (statement of the subject)."
blocks.es_reference: Transición. La transición es el paso de una sección del sermón a otra. Usted necesita una transición de la introducción al cuerpo, entre las divisiones, y al pasar de las divisiones a la conclusión. La transición mayor es la que va de la introducción al cuerpo. Esta transición debe incluir el sujeto y puede enunciarse así: «Examinemos (transición) algunas respuestas sobre quién es Cristo (enunciado del sujeto)».

blocks.en: Introduction. An introduction leads into the sermon and should comprise five to twenty percent of a sermon. The introduction seeks to gain attention, to let the people know why the sermon is important, to give the purpose of the sermon, and to establish rapport with the audience. I nearly always prepare the introduction after completing everything else. I like to know what I am introducing before putting it down. Two primary types: textual introduction (discusses geography, history, archaeology, setting and customs surrounding the text) and subject introduction (introduces the topic itself in a unique and interesting way — often by free association from a personal memory or current event).
blocks.es_reference: Título. El título es el nombre que le da al sermón — cómo se llama. El propósito principal de tener un título es para anunciar el sermón. Está tratando de captar la atención del oyente. Algunos pastores colocan el título del sermón en el letrero de la iglesia; otros lo ponen en el boletín. El título a veces puede ser igual al sujeto, pero esto no siempre es cierto. Muchos títulos efectivos se relacionan con necesidades humanas: "Cómo Criar a Sus Hijos," "Cómo Tener un Hogar Feliz," "Cómo Sobrellevar el Estrés," "Cómo Administrar Su Dinero."

blocks.en: 6.4 The Conclusion
blocks.es_reference: 6.4 La Conclusión

blocks.en: The conclusion leads out of the sermon. It should include the objective — a practical way to implement what you have said. The conclusion is not a place to introduce new material. You may restate your major ideas or draw conclusions from the points. I usually go directly from the final division into the invitation without a sharp break. Four methods:
blocks.es_reference: La conclusión conduce fuera del sermón. Debe incluir el objetivo: una manera práctica de poner en práctica lo que usted ha dicho. La conclusión no es lugar para introducir material nuevo. Puede reformular sus ideas principales o sacar conclusiones de los puntos. Yo normalmente paso directamente de la división final a la invitación sin un corte brusco. Cuatro métodos:

blocks.en:
1. The Illustration or Story Conclusion. A powerful, moving illustration right before the final appeal softens hearts and allows the Holy Spirit to speak without restraint. Roy Fish recounts Robert Ingersoll, the noted infidel, repeatedly daring his audiences to stand if any still claimed Christ — until two teenage girls rose in a midwestern theater and walked the aisle singing "Stand Up, Stand Up for Jesus," joined by almost the entire audience.
2. The Summary Conclusion. A restatement and recapitulation of the main ideas. New ideas should not be introduced. One exception: an appeal drawn directly from the text — Jesus' "Go and do likewise" at the end of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:37, NKJV).
3. The Inference Conclusion. After stating the main ideas, draw out inferences from them. From a subject "reasons for believing in the Resurrection" — empty tomb, disciples' boldness, verified appearances — infer: "Therefore we may conclude that we serve a Lord who is alive today."
4. The Prayer Conclusion. Some pastors make an appeal and then conclude with a prayer before the invitation. Effective when done well, but runs the risk of breaking the continuity of the appeal.
blocks.es_reference:
1. La Conclusión de Ilustración o Historia. Una ilustración poderosa y conmovedora justo antes del llamado final suaviza los corazones y permite al Espíritu Santo hablar sin restricción. Roy Fish narra a Robert Ingersoll, el notorio incrédulo, desafiando repetidamente a sus audiencias a ponerse de pie si alguno aún reclamaba a Cristo — hasta que dos jóvenes adolescentes se levantaron en un teatro del medio oeste y caminaron por el pasillo cantando "Firmes y Adelante," seguidas por casi toda la audiencia.
2. La Conclusión de Resumen. Una reafirmación y recapitulación de las ideas principales. No se deben introducir nuevas ideas. Una excepción: un llamado extraído directamente del texto — el "Ve, y haz tú lo mismo" de Jesús al final del Buen Samaritano (Lucas 10:37, RVG).
3. La Conclusión de Inferencia. Después de declarar las ideas principales, extraiga inferencias de ellas. De un sujeto "razones para creer en la Resurrección" — tumba vacía, audacia de los discípulos, apariciones verificadas — infiera: "Por tanto, podemos concluir que servimos a un Señor que está vivo hoy."
4. La Conclusión de Oración. Algunos pastores hacen un llamado y luego concluyen con una oración antes de la invitación. Efectivo cuando se hace bien, pero corre el riesgo de romper la continuidad del llamado.

blocks.en: 6.5 The Preaching Analysis
blocks.es_reference: 6.5 El Análisis de Predicación

blocks.en: Now that you understand the mechanics of constructing a sermon, here is one final tool: the preaching analysis. This tool will help you examine the Bible book by book and find sermonic subjects. If you do a preaching analysis of the books of the Bible, you will have enough possible sermon topics and outlines to last your complete ministry — though such an analysis of the whole Bible could very well take most of your years of ministry.
blocks.es_reference: Ahora que usted entiende la mecánica de construir un sermón, aquí tiene una última herramienta: el análisis de predicación. Esta herramienta le ayudará a examinar la Biblia libro por libro y a encontrar sujetos sermonarios. Si hace un análisis de predicación de los libros de la Biblia, tendrá suficientes posibles temas y bosquejos de sermones para durar todo su ministerio, aunque tal análisis de toda la Biblia bien podría tomar la mayoría de sus años de ministerio.

blocks.en: A preaching analysis involves going through the text and using induction to find the probing question and an outline. It is much different from a chapter or passage outline; it begins with the discovery of common concepts within the text. The concepts may cover from one to several verses. After identifying these concepts, you use an inductive approach to discover the probing question. Often the probing question will contain the subject of the passage. Sometimes there will be a probing question within a larger probing question. Beside the probing question and concepts, you may want to write the verses. After completing the analysis, you may go back and begin to form outlines. Not all the analysis outlines are suitable for preaching outlines, but they can help in formulating them. Many pastors find an analysis especially helpful when preaching consecutive sermons through a book.
blocks.es_reference: Ahora que entiende la mecánica de construir un sermón, aquí tiene una herramienta final: el análisis de predicación. Esta herramienta le ayudará a examinar la Biblia libro por libro y a encontrar sujetos sermónicos. Si hace un análisis de predicación de los libros de la Biblia, tendrá suficientes temas y bosquejos posibles de sermón para durar todo su ministerio completo — aunque tal análisis de toda la Biblia podría tomar la mayor parte de sus años de ministerio.

mc.stem: Wayne says outlines seem to be stronger and remembered more easily when each point is:
options: Five or fewer words in length
Ten to twenty words in length
A direct quotation from a verse
mc.why: Short points (five or fewer words) are easier for the congregation to remember.

mc.stem: In the Hebrews 11 outline 'Seeing the Invisible / Believing the Incredible / Doing the Impossible,' what makes it beautiful?
options: Extended parallelism where the wording matches as far as possible across all three points
Direct quotation of the entire chapter
mc.why: Each point uses three parallel words; if you draw lines top to bottom, about half the letters extend across — even the 'In/Im' sounds in the final word are similar.

mc.stem: In grammar, the active voice means:
options: The verb is at the end of the sentence
Every sentence has an exclamation point
The subject of the sentence is doing the action expressed by the verb
The sentence is in the imperative
mc.why: Active voice: subject acts. Passive voice: subject receives the action. 'John the Baptist proclaimed the arrival of Christ' (active) vs. 'The arrival of Christ was preached by John the Baptist' (passive).

mc.stem: In the Luke 15 outline (Repentance), Wayne revises 'It covered their shame / They are given privilege / Their position is restored' to:
options: It Grants Pardon / It Gives Privilege / It Gains Position
mc.why: Wayne alliterates with G-verbs (Grants/Gives/Gains) and P-nouns (Pardon/Privilege/Position), changing passive to active voice in present tense.

mc.stem: What does Wayne say about alliteration as a rule?
options: There are times when it is good to throw the rules out the window for beauty or creativity
Only allowed in English, never in Spanish
mc.why: Wayne notes the Romans 13 'Wake up! Smell the coffee! Turn on the light!' example as a time to break the parallelism rules for memorable creativity.

mc.stem: Which theological term does Wayne say most people in the pew will NOT understand without explanation?
mc.why: For most lay hearers, words like justification, sanctification, propitiation, and redemption miss the mark unless explained in simple terms.

mc.stem: The primary purpose of a sermon title, according to Wayne, is:
options: Summarizing the entire sermon in one sentence
Identifying the author of the sermon
Listing the verses that will be used
Advertising the sermon — catching the listener's attention
mc.why: The title is for advertising. It catches the listener; it does not have to be the same as the subject.

mc.stem: What is the major transition in a sermon, according to Wayne?
options: Between the introduction and the body
Between sentence one and sentence two
Between the prayer and the offering
Between the divisions and the conclusion
mc.why: Transitions occur between introduction-body, between divisions, and between divisions-conclusion. The major one is from introduction to body.

mc.stem: What percentage of the sermon should the introduction be, according to Wayne?
mc.why: 5–20%. Long enough to gain attention, establish rapport, and announce purpose; short enough not to delay the body.

mc.stem: When does Wayne usually prepare the introduction of his sermons?
mc.why: Wayne prepares the introduction last. He wants to know what he is introducing before writing it.

mc.stem: Wayne identifies four primary methods of conclusion. Which is NOT one of them?
mc.why: The four are Illustration/Story, Summary, Inference, and Prayer. Memorizing a hymn is not one of the four.

mc.stem: In the Robert Ingersoll story (cited by Roy Fish), what brought the audience to their feet?
options: Ingersoll himself converted on the spot
A pastor stood and corrected Ingersoll's arguments
Two teenage girls in the back row stood and began singing 'Stand Up, Stand Up for Jesus'
mc.why: After Ingersoll mocked Christians three times, two teenage girls began walking down the aisle singing; gradually nearly the whole audience joined them.

mc.stem: The Summary Conclusion is described by Wayne as:
options: A poem read at the end
A restatement and recapitulation of the main ideas of the sermon — no new material should be introduced here
mc.why: Restatement and recapitulation of main ideas, with no new material — except possibly an appeal drawn from the text (e.g., 'Go and do likewise' from Luke 10).

mc.stem: In Wayne's Ephesians 1 preaching analysis, what is the first introductory question he uses?
mc.why: Wayne starts with 'Who Wrote Ephesians? — Paul (1:1)' as the first introductory question.

mc.stem: What does Wayne say a preaching analysis of the whole Bible could potentially produce?
options: Enough possible sermon topics and outlines to last a complete ministry
mc.why: Such an analysis of the whole Bible could very well take most of your years of ministry — and produce enough sermon material to last all of it.

mc.stem: The course says outline points are remembered most easily when each is how long?
mc.why: Brevity aids memory — five or fewer words per point.

mc.stem: Alliteration is defined in the course as the repetition of:
mc.why: Alliteration is the repetition of a sound; it may help beauty but is not required.

mc.stem: The primary purpose of a sermon title is:
mc.why: The title advertises the sermon and catches the listener's attention.

mc.stem: The major transition in a sermon is the move from:
mc.why: The major transition is introduction-to-body, and it should include the subject.

mc.stem: The conclusion should include the objective and must never:
mc.why: The conclusion leads out of the sermon; it is not the place for new material.

The repetition of a sound in an outline is called ____.
A message is usually stronger if it is in the ____ voice instead of the passive voice.
Jesus managed to communicate important theological concepts with the use of ____.
The primary purpose for having a sermon title is for ____ the sermon, to catch the listener's attention.
The ____ is the moving from one section of the sermon to another, such as from the introduction into the body.

sa.prompt: List the three primary ingredients of 'beauty' in an outline, according to Wayne. For each, give a brief explanation and a Biblical example.
sa.model: (1) Brevity — points of five or fewer words are more easily remembered. Example: 'I shall not want' as a sub-heading rather than a paragraph. (2) Parallelism — extending the wording of each division as far as possible. Example: Hebrews 11 outline 'Seeing the Invisible / Believing the Incredible / Doing the Impossible' (three parallel words per point, even matching prefixes). (3) Active voice — the subject acts rather than receives action. Example: 'He healed them / He loved them / He fed them' from Matthew 14 rather than 'They were healed / They were loved / They were fed.' Strong answer also notes that alliteration is a tool of parallelism, not a separate rule.

sa.prompt: Take Wayne's Luke 15 outline ('It covered their shame / They are given privilege / Their position is restored') and walk through his revision step by step. What changes does he make, and what principle does each change illustrate?
sa.model: Step 1: change 'shame' (point 1) to 'pardon' to alliterate with privilege and position — illustrates ALLITERATION through P-nouns. Step 2: rewrite points 2 and 3 to active voice and present tense ('It gives privilege / It gains position') — illustrates ACTIVE VOICE and PRESENT TENSE consistency. Step 3: align all three with G-verbs (Grants / Gives / Gains) — illustrates EXTENDED PARALLELISM at the verb position. Final outline: 'It Grants Pardon / It Gives Privilege / It Gains Position.' Wayne's larger point: revision is normal — first drafts are rough, beauty comes from intentional reworking that does not change the meaning of the text.

sa.prompt: Wayne provides a Romans 13:11–12 outline ('Wake up! Smell the coffee! Turn on the light!') as a deliberate exception to his parallelism rules. Why does he include this example, and when is it appropriate to break the rules?
sa.model: Wayne includes the example because rules exist to serve memorability and beauty — when a different style serves those ends better, the rules yield. The Romans 13 outline is a sequence of imperatives that mimic a person waking up; it has no shared keyword in the noun position, breaks parallelism of grammatical structure, and yet is more memorable than a tidy alliterated outline would be. Strong answer notes: (1) the exception should be conscious, not lazy — Wayne is breaking rules deliberately, not because he didn't know them; (2) the exception should fit the tone of the text — a wake-up passage warrants a punchy, jolting outline; (3) the rules return after the exception ends — the next sermon goes back to standard form.

sa.prompt: Build a simple theological lexicon for the lay congregation: take five seminary words (e.g., justification, sanctification, propitiation, redemption, reconciliation) and provide a simple word or phrase a child could understand.
sa.model: Strong answers show clear, child-testable equivalents — not just dictionary definitions. Sample: Justification = 'God treats us as if we never sinned, because Jesus stood in our place.' Sanctification = 'Becoming more like Jesus, day by day.' Propitiation = 'Jesus took the punishment that should have been ours.' Redemption = 'God bought us back, like rescuing someone from slavery.' Reconciliation = 'Being friends with God again after a fight.' Wayne's standard: read your explanation to a child — if the child blinks, rewrite.

sa.prompt: Compare Wayne's two primary types of introduction (textual vs. subject) and give one example of when each would be preferable.
sa.model: Textual introduction: discusses matters surrounding the text — geography, history, archaeology, setting, customs. Best when the text is set in a vivid historical scene the congregation needs to picture (e.g., the Triumphal Entry sermon: 'As Jesus came into Jerusalem for the last time, he came as the Messiah, riding on a colt…'). Subject introduction: introduces the topic rather than the setting, often through free association and personal narrative (e.g., the 'fear' sermon: 'When I was a child I would wake up from nightmares, heart pounding, until I remembered my father was in the house'). Strong answers note that subject introductions work for topical sermons or for textual sermons where the subject is universal (fear, courage, forgiveness), while textual introductions work best when the historical setting itself is essential to the message.

sa.prompt: Walk through the four primary methods of conclusion that Wayne identifies. For each, give a brief description and one Biblical text where that method would fit naturally.
sa.model: (1) Illustration / Story — a moving illustration right before the appeal softens the heart and prepares for response. Fits sermons from any passage; Wayne cites the Ingersoll story (two teenage girls singing 'Stand Up, Stand Up for Jesus' until the audience joins). (2) Summary — restatement of main ideas, no new material. Fits sermons with three to five clearly numbered divisions where the congregation needs to lock the structure in memory. (3) Inference — drawing inferences from the main ideas. Fits doctrinal sermons (e.g., Resurrection: empty tomb, disciples' boldness, verified appearances → therefore, the Lord is alive today). (4) Prayer — the appeal closes with prayer rather than an invitation. Works in liturgical contexts and intimate settings; Wayne warns it can break the continuity of the appeal.

sa.prompt: Tell the Robert Ingersoll story in your own words and explain why it functions powerfully as an Illustration Conclusion. What would be lost if a preacher merely SAID 'Christians should stand for Jesus' instead of telling this story?
sa.model: Strong narration: Robert Ingersoll, a 19th-century atheist lecturer, toured midwestern cities mocking Christianity ('Why I Am Sure There Is No God,' 'The Mistakes of Moses,' 'Why Only a Fool Would Believe in Hell'). One night after his speech he challenged the audience: 'Is there even one Christian here who will testify, I still believe?' Three times he asked; three times silence; three times Ingersoll laughed. Then from a back row two teenage girls stood, moved into the aisle, and began walking forward singing 'Stand up, Stand up for Jesus.' One by one others joined them until nearly the whole audience was standing in front of the stage, singing in Ingersoll's face. What is lost in the bare statement: (1) The contrast — Ingersoll's mockery vs. the simple courage of two teenage girls; (2) The cost — Christians did stand, but only after being humiliated into silence; (3) The picture — adults followed children, which is the gospel pattern; (4) The emotional weight that prepares the hearer to respond rather than just agree. The story does what the sentence cannot: it shows the courage rather than describing it.

sa.prompt: Explain what Wayne means by a 'preaching analysis' and how it differs from a verse-by-verse exegesis. Walk through how the analysis of Ephesians 1 produces sermonic subjects that ordinary exegesis would not surface.
sa.model: A preaching analysis is an inductive scan of a book of the Bible designed to surface SERMONIC subjects — probing questions and outlines suitable for preaching — rather than to explain every verse in turn. It groups verses by concept rather than by sequence. Sample from Ephesians 1: instead of asking 'what does each verse mean?', the analyst asks 'by what means are we elected?' and lets the answer surface — by His choice (1:3), by His love (1:4b), by His pleasure and will (1:5b), by His blood (1:7), by His grace (1:7c–8). That is already a textual sermon outline. Then ask 'what are the reasons God chose us?' — to be blessed (1:3), to be holy and blameless (1:4), to praise Him (1:6), to be a workmanship (2:10). Another sermon. The analysis can produce many sermons from one chapter that ordinary commentary-style exegesis would never group together. Wayne's claim: a full preaching analysis of the whole Bible could yield enough material to preach for a complete ministry.

sa.prompt: Take a plain three-point outline of your own and beautify it: apply brevity, parallelism, and active voice. Show the outline before and after, and explain each change you made.
sa.model: Strong answer shows a clear before/after. The 'after' demonstrates brevity (five or fewer words per point), parallelism (matching grammatical form across all three), and active voice (the subject acts). Each change should be explained, not just made — e.g., 'I changed a passive phrase to active so the points match.'

sa.prompt: Choose one of the four methods of conclusion the unit describes and write a short closing for a sermon on God's forgiveness using that method. Then explain why that method fits this particular subject.
sa.model: Strong answer names one method (illustration/story, summary, inference, or direct appeal), writes a short conclusion in that style on God's forgiveness, includes the objective, introduces no new material, and explains the fit — e.g., a moving illustration softens the heart before the invitation to receive forgiveness.
